subject: general
question: According to the Supreme Court ruling in 'The State of Madhya Pradesh vs Balveer Singh' (24 February 2025) case, which of the following statements is correct regarding 'child witnesses'?

options.text: Courts must reject a child’s testimony if there is any minor inconsistency.
The Evidence Act mandates a minimum age for a person to be a witness in court.
A child’s evidence is admissible if found voluntary, reliable and untutored.
The testimony of a child witness is inadmissible unless corroborated by an adult.

solution:
The correct answer is __**A child's evidence is admissible if found voluntary, reliable and untutored.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Supreme Court in the 'State of Madhya Pradesh vs Balveer Singh' case ruled that the testimony of child witnesses is admissible if it is **voluntary, reliable, and untutored**.
 
• Courts assess the credibility of child witnesses based on the **competence and reliability** of their testimony rather than their age.
 
• Under the Indian Evidence Act, there is **no minimum age limit** for a witness; children can testify if they understand the questions and provide rational answers.
 
• Minor inconsistencies in a child's testimony do not necessarily discredit it; the courts focus on the overall truthfulness and reliability of the evidence.
 
• Judicial precedent emphasizes that corroboration is not mandatory for child witnesses if their testimony is credible and trustworthy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Child Witness:** A child witness is any individual below 18 years who provides testimony in legal proceedings.
 
• **Competency Test:** Courts conduct a competency test to evaluate whether a child witness understands the nature of an oath and can provide rational answers.
 
• **Indian Evidence Act:** Section 118 of the Act states that all persons, including children, are competent to testify provided they can comprehend and respond to questions.
 
• **Untutored Testimony:** Courts prefer untutored evidence from children to avoid influence or coaching, ensuring the authenticity of their statements.
 
• **Judicial Precedents:** Indian courts have consistently ruled that corroboration of child testimony is not essential if it is found credible and trustworthy.
